CHAPTER XXXII

In the refectory allusion was made, at the table where Gerard sat,
to the sudden death of the monk who had undertaken to write out fresh
copies of the charter of the monastery, and the rule, etc.

Gerard caught this, and timidly offered his services. There was a
hesitation which he mistook. “Nay, not for hire, my lords, but for love,
and as a trifling return for many a good night's lodging the brethren of
your order have bestowed on me a poor wayfarer.”

A monk smiled approvingly; but hinted that the late brother was an
excellent penman, and his work could not be continued but by a master.
Gerard on this drew from his wallet with some trepidation a vellum deed,
the back of which he had cleaned and written upon by way of specimen.
The monk gave quite a start at sight of it, and very hastily went up
the hall to the high table, and bending his knee so as just to touch in
passing the fifth step and the tenth, or last, presented it to the prior
with comments. Instantly a dozen knowing eyes were fixed on it, and a
buzz of voices was heard; and soon Gerard saw the prior point more than
once, and the monk came back, looking as proud as Punch, with a savoury
crustade ryal, or game pie gravied and spiced, for Gerard, and a silver
grace cup full of rich pimentum. This latter Gerard took, and bowing
low, first to the distant prior, then to his own company, quaffed, and
circulated the cup.

Instantly, to his surprise, the whole table hailed him as a brother:
“Art convent bred, deny it not?” He acknowledged it, and gave Heaven
thanks for it, for otherwise he had been as rude and ignorant as his
brothers, Sybrandt and Cornelis.

“But 'tis passing strange how you could know,” said he.

“You drank with the cup in both hands,” said two monks, speaking
together.

The voices had for some time been loudish round a table at the bottom
of the hall; but presently came a burst of mirth so obstreperous and
prolonged, that the prior sent the very sub-prior all down the hall to
check it, and inflict penance on every monk at the table. And Gerard's
cheek burned with shame; for in the heart of the unruly merriment his
ear had caught the word “courage!” and the trumpet tones of Denys of
Burgundy.

Soon Gerard was installed in feu Werter's cell, with wax lights, and a
little frame that could be set at any angle, and all the materials of
caligraphy. The work, however, was too much for one evening. Then came
the question, how could he ask Denys, the monk-hater, to stay longer?
However, he told him, and offered to abide by his decision. He was
agreeably surprised when Denys said graciously, “A day's rest will do
neither of us harm. Write thou, and I'll pass the time as I may.”

Gerard's work was vastly admired; they agreed that the records of the
monastery had gained by poor Werter's death. The sub-prior forced a
rix-dollar on Gerard, and several brushes and colours out of the convent
stock, which was very large. He resumed his march warm at heart, for
this was of good omen; since it was on the pen he relied to make
his fortune and recover his well-beloved. “Come, Denys,” said he
good-humouredly, “see what the good monks have given me; now, do try to
be fairer to them; for to be round with you, it chilled my friendship
for a moment to hear even you call my benefactors 'hypocrites.'”

“I recant,” said Denys.

“Thank you! thank you! Good Denys.”

“I was a scurrilous vagabond.”

“Nay, nay, say not so, neither!”

“But we soldiers are rude and hasty. I give myself the lie, and I offer
those I misunderstood all my esteem. 'Tis unjust that thousands should
be defamed for the hypocrisy of a few.”

“Now are you reasonable. You have pondered what I said?”

“Nay, it is their own doing.”

Gerard crowed a little, we all like to be proved in the right; and
was all attention when Denys offered to relate how his conversion was
effected.

“Well then, at dinner the first day a young monk beside me did open his
jaws and laughed right out and most musically. 'Good,' said I, 'at last
I have fallen on a man and not a shorn ape.' So, to sound him further,
I slapped his broad back and administered my consigne. 'Heaven forbid!'
says he. I stared. For the dog looked as sad as Solomon; a better mime
saw you never, even at a Mystery. 'I see war is no sharpener of the
wits,' said he. 'What are the clergy for but to fight the foul fiend?
and what else are the monks for?

     “The fiend being dead,
     The friars are sped.”

You may plough up the convents, and we poor monks shall have nought to
do--but turn soldiers, and so bring him to life again.' Then there was a
great laugh at my expense. 'Well, you are the monk for me,' said I. 'And
you are the crossbowman for me,' quo' he. 'And I'll be bound you could
tell us tales of the war should make our hair stand on end.' 'Excusez!
the barber has put that out of the question,' quoth I, and then I had
the laugh.”

“What wretched ribaldry!” observed Gerard pensively.

The candid Denys at once admitted he had seen merrier jests hatched with
less cackle. “'Twas a great matter to have got rid of hypocrisy. 'So,'
said I, 'I can give you the chaire de poule, if that may content ye.'
'That we will see,' was the cry, and a signal went round.”

Denys then related, bursting with glee, how at bedtime he had been taken
to a cell instead of the great dortour, and strictly forbidden to sleep;
and to aid his vigil, a book had been lent him of pictures representing
a hundred merry adventures of monks in pursuit of the female laity;
and how in due course he had been taken out barefooted and down to the
parlour, where was a supper fit for the duke, and at it twelve jolly
friars, the roaringest boys he had ever met in peace or war. How the
story, the toast, the jest, the wine-cup had gone round, and some
had played cards with a gorgeous pack, where Saint Theresa, and Saint
Catherine, etc., bedizened with gold, stood for the four queens; and
black, white, grey, and crutched friars for the four knaves; and had
staked their very rosaries, swearing like troopers when they lost. And
how about midnight a sly monk had stolen out, but had by him and others
been as cannily followed into the garden, and seen to thrust his hand
into the ivy and out with a rope-ladder. With this he had run up on
the wall, which was ten feet broad, yet not so nimbly but what a russet
kirtle had popped up from the outer world as quick as he; and so to
billing and cooing: that this situation had struck him as rather feline
than ecclesiastical, and drawn from him the appropriate comment of a
“mew!” The monks had joined the mewsical chorus, and the lay visitor
shrieked and been sore discomforted; but Abelard only cried, “What, are
ye there, ye jealous miauling knaves? ye shall caterwaul to some tune
to-morrow night. I'll fit every man-jack of ye with a fardingale.” That
this brutal threat had reconciled him to stay another day--at Gerard's
request.

Gerard groaned.

Meantime, unable to disconcert so brazen a monk, and the demoiselle
beginning to whimper, they had danced caterwauling in a circle, then
bestowed a solemn benediction on the two wall-flowers, and off to
the parlour, where they found a pair lying dead drunk, and other
two affectionate to tears. That they had straightway carried off the
inanimate, and dragged off the loving and lachymose, kicked them all
merrily each into his cell.

“And so shut up in measureless content.”

Gerard was disgusted: and said so.

Denys chuckled, and proceeded to tell him how the next day he and the
young monks had drawn the fish-ponds and secreted much pike, carp,
tench, and eel for their own use: and how, in the dead of night, he had
been taken shoeless by crooked ways into the chapel, a ghost-like place,
being dark, and then down some steps into a crypt below the chapel
floor, where suddenly paradise had burst on him.

“'Tis there the holy fathers retire to pray,” put in Gerard.

“Not always,” said Denys; “wax candles by the dozen were lighted, and
princely cheer; fifteen soups maigre, with marvellous twangs of venison,
grouse, and hare in them, and twenty different fishes (being Friday),
cooked with wondrous art, and each he between two buxom lasses, and each
lass between two lads with a cowl; all but me: and to think I had to woo
by interpreter. I doubt the knave put in three words for himself and
one for me; if he didn't, hang him for a fool. And some of the weaker
vessels were novices, and not wont to hold good wine; had to be coaxed
ere they would put it to their white teeth; mais elles s'y faisaient;
and the story, and the jest, and the cup went round (by-the-by, they had
flagons made to simulate breviaries); and a monk touched the cittern,
and sang ditties with a voice tunable as a lark in spring. The posies
did turn the faces of the women folk bright red at first: but elles s'y
faisaient.”

Here Gerard exploded.

“Miserable wretches! Corrupters of youth! Perverters of innocence! but
for your being there, Denys, who have been taught no better, oh,
would God the church had fallen on the whole gang. Impious, abominable
hypocrites!”

“Hypocrites?” cried Denys, with unfeigned surprise. “Why, that is what I
clept them ere I knew them: and you withstood me. Nay, they are sinners;
all good fellows are that; but, by St. Denys his helmeted skull, no
hypocrites, but right jolly roaring blades.”

“Denys,” said Gerard solemnly, “you little know the peril you ran that
night. That church you defiled amongst you is haunted; I had it from
one of the elder monks. The dead walk there, their light feet have been
heard to patter o'er the stones.”

“Misericorde!” whispered Denys.

“Ay, more,” said Gerard, lowering his voice almost to a whisper;
“celestial sounds have issued from the purlieus of that very crypt you
turned into a tavern. Voices of the dead holding unearthly communion
have chilled the ear of midnight, and at times, Denys, the faithful in
their nightly watches have even heard music from dead lips; and chords,
made by no mortal finger, swept by no mortal hand, have rung faintly,
like echoes, deep among the dead in those sacred vaults.”

Denys wore a look of dismay. “Ugh! if I had known, mules and wain-ropes
had not hauled me thither; and so” (with a sigh) “I had lost a merry
time.”

Whether further discussion might have thrown any more light upon these
ghostly sounds, who can tell? for up came a “bearded brother” from the
monastery, spurring his mule, and waving a piece of vellum in his hand.
It was the deed between Ghysbrecht and Floris Brandt. Gerard valued it
deeply as a remembrance of home: he turned pale at first but to think he
had so nearly lost it, and to Denys's infinite amusement not only gave a
piece of money to the lay brother, but kissed the mule's nose.

“I'll read you now,” said Gerard, “were you twice as ill written;
and--to make sure of never losing you”--here he sat down, and taking out
needle and thread, sewed it with feminine dexterity to his doublet, and
his mind, and heart, and soul were away to Sevenbergen.

They reached the promised land, and Denys, who was in high spirits,
doffed his bonnet to all the females; who curtsied and smiled in return;
fired his consigne at most of the men; at which some stared, some
grinned, some both; and finally landed his friend at one of the
long-promised Burgundian inns.

“It is a little one,” said he, “but I know it of old for a good one;
Les Trois Poissons.' But what is this writ up? I mind not this;” and he
pointed to an inscription that ran across the whole building in a single
line of huge letters. “Oh, I see. 'Ici on loge a pied et a cheval,'”
 said Denys, going minutely through the inscription, and looking
bumptious when he had effected it.

Gerard did look, and the sentence in question ran thus:

“ON NE LOGE CEANS A CREDIT; CE BONHOMME EST MORT, LES MAUVAIS PAIEURS
L'ONT TUE.”

[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

Before I had traversed fifty paces, a sudden rupture of lightning tore the sky, pursued instantly by a shriek so guttural it arrested my breath. It was a sound stripped of all former sovereignty. I could not trace its origin through the howling wind, but then I heard the voice—his voice, diminished and frantic—commanding my return.

I obeyed, stepping back over the jagged stone, and found him frozen exactly where I had left him.

"You called me, master?" I asked, testing the word on my tongue.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

They reached the promised land, and Denys, who was in high spirits, doffed his bonnet to all the females; who curtsied and smiled in return; fired his consigne at most of the men; at which some stared, some grinned, some both; and finally landed his friend at one of the long-promised Burgundian inns. “It is a little one,” said he, “but I know it of old for a good one; Les Trois Poissons.' But what is this writ up? I mind not this;” and he pointed to an inscription that ran across the whole building in a single line of huge letters. “Oh, I see. 'Ici on loge a pied et a cheval,'” said Denys, going minutely through the inscription, and looking bumptious when he had effected it. Gerard did look, and the sentence in question ran thus: “ON NE LOGE CEANS A CREDIT; CE BONHOMME EST MORT, LES MAUVAIS PAIEURS L'ONT TUE.”

In the dim, candlelit expanse of the refectory, where the air hung thick with the scent of stale bread and incense, conversation drifted toward the sudden vacancy at the scriptorium. A monk spoke of the brother who had perished—a victim of fate or fever—who had been entrusted with the monumental task of transcribing the monastery's charter and rule. The news rippled through the assembly until it reached Gerard, whose heart leaped with a mixture of terror and hope. Rising with trembling knees, he offered his services, his voice barely audible above the rustle of habits.

"Nay, not for hire, my lords," he pleaded, his eyes darting nervously to the high table, "but for love. As a trifling return for the countless nights of shelter the brethren of your order have bestowed upon this poor wayfarer."

A murmur of approval rose from the lower ranks, but a senior monk, his face lined with skepticism, shook his head. "The late brother was a master of the pen," he intoned, his tone carrying the weight of institutional tradition. "His work cannot be continued save by a master. Your skill, stranger, is unknown here."

Gerard felt the heat rise in his cheeks. From the folds of his tunic, he drew forth a vellum deed, the back of which he had painstakingly cleaned and inscribed with a flourish of his own making—a specimen of his craft. He held it out, his fingers stiff.

The monk's reaction was instantaneous. His eyes widened, the skepticism evaporating into awe. He snatched the document, his movements jerky with excitement, and hurried up the long hall to the high table. Bending his knee, he brushed against the fifth and tenth steps—the sacred thresholds of the Prior's domain—and presented the deed with a reverence usually reserved for relics.

Instantly, the atmosphere shifted. A dozen knowing eyes locked onto the page, and a low hum of voices erupted, growing into a buzz of speculation. Gerard watched, breathless, as the Prior pointed repeatedly at the script, his finger tracing the elegant curves of the ink. The senior monk returned, his face flushed with triumph, bearing a savory *crustade royale* and a game pie spiced with exotic herbs for Gerard, alongside a silver grace cup brimming with rich *pimentum*.

Gerard accepted the feast, bowed low first to the distant Prior, then to his new companions, and raised the cup. As he quaffed and passed it along, a transformation occurred. The hostility dissolved; the table hailed him as kin.

"Art convent-bred? Deny it not?" the voices demanded in unison.

Gerard acknowledged the truth, giving silent thanks to Heaven. Without this revelation, he would have remained as rough and ignorant as his fellow travelers, Sybrandt and Cornelis.

"But 'tis passing strange how you could know," the Prior remarked, leaning forward.

"You drank with the cup in both hands," two monks chimed in, their laughter ringing clear.

For some time, the lower tables had been the source of raucous noise, but now a burst of mirth so obstreperous and prolonged threatened to tear the roof from the hall. The Prior, losing patience, dispatched the Sub-Prior to quell the uproar and impose penance upon the riotous monks. Yet, amidst the chaos, Gerard's face burned with shame. In the heart of the unruly revelry, his ear had caught a specific word—"courage!"—and the trumpet-toned voice of Denys of Burgundy cutting through the din.

Soon, Gerard was settled in Feu Werter's cell. Wax lights flickered against the stone walls, illuminating a small easel capable of adjusting to any angle, surrounded by the finest materials of calligraphy. Yet, the work proved too arduous for a single evening. The question gnawed at him: how could he ask Denys, the self-proclaimed monk-hater, to remain longer?

He approached Denys, offering to abide by whatever decision the soldier wished. To his delight, Denys responded with unexpected grace. "A day's rest will do neither of us harm. Write thou, and I'll pass the time as I may."

Gerard's work was swiftly admired. The community agreed that the monastery's records had suffered a grievous loss with poor Werter's death. The Sub-Prior pressed a rix-dollar into Gerard's hand, along with brushes and pigments from the convent's ample stores. Warm-hearted and buoyed by this good omen, Gerard believed his fortune—and his recovery of his well-beloved—lay in the power of the pen.

"Come, Denys," he said, his demeanor lightening, "see what the good monks have given me. Now, do try to be fairer to them; for to be round with you, it chilled my friendship for a moment to hear even you call my benefactors 'hypocrites.'"

"I recant," Denys declared immediately.

"Thank you! Thank you! Good Denys."

"I was a scurrilous vagabond."

"Nay, nay, say not so!"

"But we soldiers are rude and hasty. I give myself the lie, and I offer those I misunderstood all my esteem. 'Tis unjust that thousands should be defamed for the hypocrisy of a few."

"Now you are reasonable. Have you pondered what I said?"

"Nay, it is their own doing."

Gerard crowed softly, for everyone delights in being proven right, and listened intently as Denys recounted the genesis of his conversion.

"Well then," Denys began, his voice animated, "at dinner the first day, a young monk beside me opened his jaws and laughed right out, most musically. 'Good,' said I, 'at last I have fallen on a man and not a shorn ape.' So, to sound him further, I slapped his broad back and administered my consigne. 'Heaven forbid!' says he. I stared. For the dog looked as sad as Solomon; a better mime you never saw, even at a Mystery play. 'I see war is no sharpener of the wits,' he replied. 'What are the clergy for but to fight the foul fiend? and what else are the monks for? "The fiend being dead, The friars are sped." You may plough up the convents, and we poor monks shall have nought to do—but turn soldiers, and so bring him to life again.' Then there was a great laugh at my expense. 'Well, you are the monk for me,' said I. 'And you are the crossbowman for me,' quoth he. 'And I'll be bound you could tell us tales of the war should make our hair stand on end.' 'Excusez! the barber has put that out of the question,' quoth I, and then I had the laugh."

"What wretched ribaldry!" Gerard observed, his brow furrowing pensively.

The candid Denys admitted at once that he had witnessed merrier jests hatched with less cacophony. "'Twas a great matter to have got rid of hypocrisy," he continued. "'So,' said I, 'I can give you the chaire de poule, if that may content ye.' 'That we will see,' was the cry, and a signal went round."

Then Denys burst into a tale of glee regarding his bedtime. Instead of the great dormitory, he had been ushered into a private cell, strictly forbidden to sleep. To aid his vigil, a book of pictures depicting a hundred merry adventures of monks pursuing the female laity was lent to him. In due course, he was taken barefoot down to the parlour, where a supper fit for a duke awaited. Twelve jolly friars, the roaringest boys he had ever met in peace or war, sat around the table. The story, the toast, the jest, and the wine-cup circulated freely. Some played cards with a gorgeous pack where Saint Theresa and Saint Catherine, bedizened with gold, stood for the four queens; while black, white, grey, and crutched friars represented the four knaves. They staked their very rosaries, swearing like troopers when they lost.

At midnight, a sly monk stole out, only to be cunningly followed by others into the garden, where he was seen thrusting his hand into the ivy and pulling out a rope-ladder. He scaled the ten-foot wall with such nimbleness that a russet kirtle popped up from the outer world as quickly as he. Thus began a scene of billing and cooing that struck Denys as rather feline than ecclesiastical, drawing from him the appropriate comment of a "mew!" The monks joined the musical chorus, and the lay visitor shrieked in discomfort. But Abelard merely cried, "What, are ye there, ye jealous miauling knaves? Ye shall caterwaul to some tune tomorrow night. I'll fit every man-jack of ye with a fardingale."

This brutal threat had reconciled Denys to staying another day—at Gerard's request. Gerard groaned inwardly. Meanwhile, unable to disconcert such a brazen monk, and the demoiselle beginning to whimper, they had danced caterwauling in a circle before bestowing a solemn benediction on the two wall-flowers and retreating to the parlour. There, they found a pair lying dead drunk and two others affectionate to tears. They had straightway carried off the inanimate bodies, dragged the loving and lachrymose ones kicking and screaming into their cells, and shut them up in measureless content.
